body_markdown:
Two healthcare careers that often provide stable employment opportunities and rewarding career experiences are dental assisting and medical assisting.


Both allow you to work directly with patients, support healthcare professionals, and perform essential work that is needed and appreciated. But how do you choose which path to take? Consider your own interests, check out what each career could offer, and find out how to go from where you are now to a real healthcare career.


## Would You Prefer Dental Assisting or Medical Assisting?


Whether you want to[become a dental assistant](https://www.lincolntech.edu/news/health-sciences/dental-assistant/how-to-become-a-dental-assistant) or a medical assistant, you need to have compassion, attention to detail, good communication skills, and a desire to help others. But you may already lean toward one role over the other. Maybe you actually like going to the dentist. Or maybe you’ve seen a medical assistant be the hero in a loved one’s time of need. Let your own interests and strengths guide you.


*Dental assisting* may be a good fit if you:


- Are interested in teeth, oral health, and dentistry
- Enjoy precise, detail-oriented work
- Like working with your hands and using specialized tools and equipment
- Prefer working closely with the same dentist or dental team
- Are comfortable working in a focused, specialized healthcare environment
- Enjoy helping patients feel at ease during procedures


*Medical assisting* may be a good fit if you:


- Are interested in the human body, health, and medicine
- Like variety and want to perform different clinical and administrative tasks
- Enjoy interacting with patients with a wide range of healthcare needs
- Would be okay taking vitals, drawing blood, collecting specimens
- Want to work in settings like physician offices, clinics, and healthcare facilities
- Can stay organized while moving between multiple responsibilities
- Could accurately maintain medical records


## What Does a Dental Assistant Do?


As a dental assistant, you work alongside dentists and dental hygienists to help provide oral healthcare and keep dental practices running smoothly. On one side, you’re a second set of hands in the exam room creating[four-handed dentistry](https://www.lincolntech.edu/news/health-sciences/dental-assistant/what-is-four-handed-dentistry) that cares for the patient. But you also work in the front office handling administrative responsibilities.


Depending on the practice and state regulations, you might:


- Prepare patients for procedures
- Assist the dentist during appointments
- Sterilize instruments and equipment
- Take dental X-rays
- Maintain patient records
- Schedule appointments
- Teach patients about oral care


Your work environment is predictable and consistent. About[90% of dental assistants worked in dentists' offices](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/healthcare/dental-assistants.htm#tab-3) .


## What Does a Medical Assistant Do?


As a medical assistant, you support more patients in a broader healthcare environment. You work with physicians and other healthcare professionals and may also divide your time between clinical and administrative responsibilities. Your responsibilities include:


- Take vital signs
- Prepare patients for exams
- Collect specimens
- Draw blood
- Administer medications
- Assist with procedures
- Schedule appointments
- Updating electronic health records
- Communicate with patients


Your work environment as a medical assistant isn’t just a single setting. While[most medical assistants work in doctors’ offices](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/healthcare/medical-assistants.htm#tab-3) , you might also work in a hospital, clinic, outpatient care center, or long-term care facility. This variety can make medical assisting appealing if you want to build skills that apply across different areas of healthcare.


## Dental Assistant vs. Medical Assistant Training


Neither career requires a four-year college degree. Certificate programs can teach you the skills you need for entry-level work, although licensing varies by state. The difference between medical and dental assistant training is what you learn.


Dental assistant training focuses on oral healthcare. Typical classroom and hands-on instruction include lessons in:


- Chairside assisting
- Four-handed dentistry
- Oral anatomy
- Infection control and sterilization
- Dental radiography
- Dental impressions
- Restorative dentistry
- Periodontics
- Oral surgery
- Dental office procedures


Medical assistant training covers a broader range of medical care. You will generally learn:


- Anatomy and physiology
- Medical terminology Vital signs
- Patient preparation
- Infection control and sterilization
- Phlebotomy and specimen collection
- Electronic health records
- Medication administration
- Medical office procedures


What you need to[look for in a medical assistant school](https://www.lincolntech.edu/news/health-sciences/medical-assistant/look-for-medical-assistant-school) or[dental assistant school](https://www.lincolntech.edu/news/health-sciences/dental-assistant/what-look-dental-assistant-school) is similar. The school and its programs need to be accredited, offering modern facilities with the same kind of equipment and tools you find in the real world. And hands-on training taught by professionals from the field is a must. Programs for either career should also include opportunities to apply your newly built skills in real healthcare environments through internships.


## The Job Outlook for Dental Assistants


Demand for dental assistants is higher than average with a 6 percent growth rate predicted through 20341. More than 50,000 dental assistant job openings are projected each year over the decade2.


## The Job Outlook for Medical Assistants


Medical assisting is projected to grow even faster. Employment is expected to increase 12% through 20343, with more than 112,000 openings projected annually4.


## Earnings for Dental and Medical Assistants


[Salaries for dental assistants](https://www.lincolntech.edu/news/health-sciences/dental-assistant/dental-assistant-salary-guide-what-could-you-earn) and[medical assistants](https://www.lincolntech.edu/news/health-sciences/medical-assistant/medical-assistant-salary-guide-how-much-can-you-earn) vary depending on where you live, but according to US Bureau of Labor Statistics, the median wage for dental assistants was $47,300 in May 20245 and the salary for medical assistants was $44,2006.


## Dental Assistant or Medical Assistant: Which Is Right for You?


Whether a dental assistant or medical assistant career is right for you depends mostly on the type of work environment and patient care that interests you.


Dental assisting is a good fit if you are interested in oral health, like detailed hands-on work, and can picture yourself working closely with a dentist in a dental practice. You may enjoy the opportunity to become skilled in a clearly defined area of healthcare.


Medical assisting might be a fit if you want broader exposure to healthcare. Because medical assistants can perform both clinical and administrative tasks and work in several types of healthcare facilities, the career offers opportunities to experience different aspects of patient care.


In either case, communication, compassion, attention to detail, and comfort working closely with patients can help you succeed.
